entries.detail:
Here are the Phase 1 acceptance criteria and my plan for batch 1. I haven't written or changed any files yet.

## Phase 1 acceptance criteria
- **AC1.1:** `data/institutions.csv` has at least 35 rows, unique slugs, and a valid `type` (`private_r1 | public_r1 | other`). Columns are `slug,name,type,state,cs_dept_url`.
- **AC1.2:** Every slug has a `data/raw/<slug>.md` file with all 5 section headers: `dept_statement`, `university_guidance`, `intro_course`, `se_course` and `notes`.
- **AC1.3:** Every section has a `url:` line that is either an http(s) URL or `not_found`/`blocked`.
- **AC1.4:** Every section with a URL has at least one `>` verbatim quote block.
- **AC1.5:** At least 70% of institutions have a URL for `dept_statement` or `university_guidance`.
- **AC1.6:** At least 50% of institutions have a URL for `se_course`.
- **AC1.7 (manual):** You open 5 random URLs and confirm the quotes match, and the result is logged in PROGRESS.md.

## Plan
1. **Build `data/institutions.csv` for all 42 seed schools.** I'll fill in slug, name, type, state and CS department URL, so the AC1.1 test can pass now.
2. **Write `tests/test_phase1_data.py`, with one test per AC and descriptive names.** The tests for AC1.2–AC1.4 run once for each raw file. Two tests look at the whole sample: the AC1.5/AC1.6 coverage thresholds and the "every slug has a raw file" check. Those two will **fail until all 4 batches are done**. That's expected, and I'll report them as pending rather than as broken.
3. **Collect batch 1:** MIT, Stanford, CMU, UC Berkeley, UIUC, Georgia Tech, UW, Cornell, Princeton and Harvard. For each school I'll search for sources in the spec's order: department statement, then university guidance, then a CS1/CS2 syllabus, then the SE course syllabus. I'll prefer the most recent term (Fall 2026 or Spring 2026).
   - **Keeping quotes verbatim:** WebFetch passes pages through a summarizing model, so its "quotes" can be quietly paraphrased. I'll use WebSearch only to find URLs. I'll get the actual text with `requests` + BeautifulSoup and copy excerpts from that output. A small helper, `scripts/check_quotes.py`, will refetch each URL and confirm every `>` block appears in the page text (ignoring whitespace differences). That gives AC1.7 an automated pre-check.
   - If a page is blocked (login wall or 403), I'll record `blocked` and try one alternative source, as the spec says. If I can't find a source, I'll record `not_found` and won't guess.
   - When a section has more than one source (for example, two intro syllabi), I'll repeat the `url:` line and quote block inside that section.
4. **Log and stop:** I'll run pytest and add timestamped entries to PROGRESS.md: your instruction as `[Adi]`, and the batch result and test counts as `[Claude]`. Then I'll stop so you can review or /clear.

## Open points (I'll go with these defaults unless you say otherwise)
- **Multiple sources per section:** handled by repeating the `url:` + quote pair, as in step 3.
- **Restricted pages:** syllabi behind Canvas or other logins count as `blocked`. I won't try to get around the login.

Reply "go" to start batch 1.

I wrote `data/raw/mit.md` and `data/raw/stanford.md`. `check_quotes.py` reports 0 missing for both: mit 9 matched, stanford 8 matched, nothing unverifiable. I touched no other files.

**mit** (`data/raw/mit.md`)
- dept_statement: not_found. A site-restricted search of eecs.mit.edu turned up only news articles. The MIT Academic Integrity handbook's code page doesn't mention AI.
- university_guidance: found two sources.
  - https://aiandeducation.mit.edu/report/ is the August 2026 report of the Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training. It says there should be no one-size-fits-all rule, every subject needs a clear policy in its syllabus, and AI detectors shouldn't be relied on.
  - https://tll.mit.edu/teaching-resources/course-design/ai-in-teaching-learning/acceptable-ai-use-policies/ is the Teaching + Learning Lab's menu of four policy options.
- intro_course: 6.100, Fall 2026, https://introcomp.mit.edu/fall26/information. AI is allowed as a tutor and to discuss approaches, but not to generate assignment code ("treat using them like talking with other people").
- se_course: 6.102 (6.1020) Software Construction, Spring 2026, https://web.mit.edu/6.102/www/sp26/general/collaboration.html. Using generative AI to write text or code is forbidden. I found no fa26 page (404); the course appears to run in spring only.

**stanford** (`data/raw/stanford.md`)
- dept_statement: not_found. Policy is set course by course on each course's honor-code page, and my guessed cs.stanford.edu honor-code URLs all returned 404.
- university_guidance: https://communitystandards.stanford.edu/generative-ai-policy-guidance. By default, AI is allowed for practice and study ("human tutor" rule of thumb). Using it to create deliverables is not allowed, and uses beyond the permitted ones must be disclosed.
- intro_course: three sources.
  - CS106B, Autumn 2026 (archive code 1272), honor code page and syllabus page. You may ask AI for general help but may not share assignment code or questions with it.
  - CS106A syllabus, https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs106a/handouts_w2021/syllabus-cs106a.html. No AI for homework, though looking up a two-line phrase is fine.
- se_course: blocked. CS194 (Winter 2027) keeps its syllabus on Canvas. I tried CS190 as the alternative, but its page is from Winter 2024 and doesn't mention AI, so I didn't use it.

**Doubtful points** (all recorded in each file's notes)
- The Stanford university guidance says it is "intended to replace" the February 2023 guidance "upon formal adoption by the BCA", so it may not be formally adopted yet.
- The CS106A syllabus page has no date. "Week 9, Nov 16" fits Autumn 2026, but the URL path says w2021, so the term isn't certain.
- The two CS106B pages disagree slightly: the honor code allows general AI help, while the syllabus says programs must not be developed with AI help.
- Stanford's se_course is blocked rather than found.

**Gotcha for future collection runs:** in zsh, `set -- $pair` doesn't split on spaces, so a loop written that way passes "url slug" as a single argument. That caused false HTTP 404s. Pass the URL and slug as separate arguments.

Page text I worked from is in `<scratchpad>/8a9578c8-e363-4116-8177-bfe3765d65ec/scratchpad/pages/`.

It is a template: courses opt in and fill in their own list of graded work where AI is allowed.

- **se_course: found.** CS 5150 Software Engineering, Spring 2026: https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs5150/2026sp/syllabus.html — AI is allowed for coding with disclosure and banned on in-class exams. CS 5150 is a Master's-level course, and I found no Fall 2026 page (404). CS 3152's Spring 2026 integrity page also has an AI policy; it is mentioned in the notes but not used.

- Cornell's SE source is a Master's-level course, not an undergraduate one.

I wrote both files. UIUC passes check_quotes with 0 missing. Georgia Tech has 0 missing, but its two course syllabi exist only as PDFs, so the checker can't verify those 4 quotes.

**uiuc** (`data/raw/uiuc.md`). check_quotes: 10 matched, 0 missing, 0 unverifiable.
- **dept_statement: not_found.** The Siebel School's undergraduate policies page and FAQ have no AI policy, and the only AI page on the school's site is a news article about research.
- **university_guidance: found, 2 sources.**
  - The teaching center's "Teaching with AI" page (citl.illinois.edu/generative-artificial-intelligence-gen-ai/teaching-implications): instructors set AI boundaries in their syllabus, and blanket bans are advised against.
  - The campus IT office's GenAI best-practices page (genai.illinois.edu/best-practices-teaching-and-learning/).
  - The University of Illinois System's "Generative AI Guidance for Instructors" page (vpaa.uillinois.edu) returned 403, so it isn't used.
- **intro_course: found, 2 courses, both Fall 2026.**
  - CS 124 (cs124.org/syllabus): homework and quizzes must be written without AI. The independent project requires students to buy Claude Pro and have Claude Code write most of the code.
  - CS 128 (cs128.org/syllabus): AI may help with the process but may not produce the code you submit. "Vibe coding" is banned. Any AI use requires a reflection form plus the full transcript.
- **se_course: blocked.** CS 427's course pages for Fall 2026 and Spring 2026 only link to Coursera, which needs a login. The one alternative I tried, CS 428's Fall 2026 page, is just a lecture list with no AI mention.

**gatech** (`data/raw/gatech.md`). check_quotes: 6 matched, 0 missing, 4 unverifiable (all 4 are from the PDF syllabi).
- **dept_statement: found, but weak.** I found no official AI policy for the whole College of Computing. The source is a College news article (cc.gatech.edu/news/new-policies-navigate-role-ai-assistants-cs-courses). It reproduces the AI policy David Joyner wrote for his own courses, so it is a course-level policy published by the college. This needs your judgment: you may prefer to code it as not_found.
- **university_guidance: found.** Two pages from Georgia Tech's IT office, oit.gatech.edu/node/481 and oit.gatech.edu/ai/genai. The Provost has a draft Institute AI policy open for feedback, but I couldn't get the draft text, so it isn't quoted.
- **intro_course: found.** CS 1331 Fall 2026 syllabus PDF on syllabus.gatech.edu. It strictly prohibits ChatGPT and other AI tools on all graded work; offenders get a zero and are reported to the Office of Student Integrity.
- **se_course: found.** CS 2340 Spring 2026 syllabus PDF (2340-spr26.pdf, Nimisha Roy). AI is allowed for brainstorming, but submitting AI content counts as misconduct, and AI tools that insert code into the editor (like Copilot) are banned. The term comes from the filename, since the PDF text doesn't state it.

**Doubtful points**
- **The 4 PDF quotes:** I pulled the text from the downloaded PDFs with pypdf, installed only in the scratchpad, not the project. All 4 quotes match that text. The only difference is that PDF line breaks split "code-generation" and "concepts—similar", which I wrote as single words. The notes in `gatech.md` explain this.
- **No HTML alternative:** I couldn't find a web-page version of either syllabus with an AI policy. cs1331.github.io doesn't mention AI, and the syllabus pages on syllabus.gatech.edu are just links to PDFs. A Fall CS 1301 PDF also has an AI policy, but its text came out garbled, so I didn't quote it.

I didn't touch any other project files.

<pasted_content id="c26c">
niversity of Michigan’s GenAI offerings
With the rise of numerous GenAI-based tools, it is important to know how to choose a tool that works best for you. Tools provided by the University of Michigan, such as U-M GPT are private, secure, accessible, equitable, and free for faculty. Data you share while using these tools will not be used for training these models, and hence are not at risk of being leaked. Look for the umich.edu domain in the page link to verify that you are using a U-M website.

U-M Generative AI Training and Events
Extensive Generative AI training is available at U-M at varying levels. Register for the ITS/TCC Generative AI workshop series or watch the series on demand. For additional events, visit the GenAI events page. Resources and training are also available for prompt literacy.

Learn more about the many AI-focused initiatives, centers, and resources across U-M:

AI Institutes at Michigan (AIIM)
MIDAS
AI Lab
AI & Digital Health Innovation
 
Academic/Teaching Implications
Because large language models can write so quickly and competently, they can assist students in completing many common types of assessments. Text outputs from language models can be used to answer essay questions, write papers, and reply to discussion board posts, simulating recall and understanding with little effort or engagement. How quickly can GenAI answer an essay question? Faster than you’d think.

Language models generalize and summarize existing knowledge based on probability predictions of word sequences rather than copying it verbatim, and so it may be impossible to identify their use with certainty. While detection tools like Turnitin or GPTZero may report probability of AI authorship, they are easily circumvented and cannot provide definitive proof of cheating. False positives and negatives are possible, and even likely. U-M does not recommend the use of AI-detection technology at this time given their high error rate.

It can be expected that U-M students are aware of these tools and many are using them for academic and non-academic purposes. Given the rapid evolution of the technology and its adaptation, this page is focused on offering near-term recommendations. Our response to GenAI should be consistent with our core values of fairness, diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, research veracity, and ethical integrity.

GenAI will create new opportunities across the entire spectrum of research activities, ranging from the natural sciences, social science, economics and political sciences, humanities, engineering, biomedical and clinical sciences, as well as the creative arts. Visit the Resources for Research page for more information.

As instructors look to future semesters, we recommend the following tasks to prepare.

Note: these tasks are also discussed in the Getting Started with Generative Artificial Intelligence: U-M Instructor guide

Evaluate if you need to make changes to your course and assessment practices
AI augmentation refers to the utilization of artificial intelligence to assist, expedite, enhance, and in some cases, substitute for humans in accomplishing tasks. AI augmentation will significantly alter the education landscape, we will need to re-evaluate teaching strategies to take advantage of the opportunities and mitigate risks.

Further, the rapid integration of AI in various sectors of society requires a re-evaluation of curriculum design to prepare students for a future where AI will be ubiquitous. Given the rapid evolution of the technology and its adaptation, this section is focused on offering near-term recommendations.

Key components of courses will have to be reviewed in relation to GenAI capacities and risks. Instructors should at minimum be able to answer the following questions about each course:

Should GenAI be used in the course or not—and why or why not?
If GenAI is to be used, how is the use to be documented?
Should course learning objectives be revised?
Should GenAI competencies be taught in the specific disciplinary context?
Should assessments be revised?
Read more about redesigning assessments

Read more about GenAI Implications for Writing and Other Disciplines

Explore a book guide on methods to incorporate Chatbots into class assignments.

Find additional resources on GenAI considerations for teaching and learning on the Academic Technology@Michigan site.

Draft a syllabus statement
First familiarize yourself with any revised academic integrity policies from your school/college. Then draft a statement in your syllabus on acceptable uses of GenAI in your classroom.

Read more about course policies and example syllabi statements

Talk with Students about Generative AI Early and Often
We encourage instructors to set aside time early in the term to tell students directly about course policies regarding GenAI usage, reasons for this decision, and what potential consequences may look like when policies are not followed. We also suggest instructors include language about GenAI in the class orientation content of Canvas courses. Use the following pointers to hold a conversation with your students about the ethical and practical implications of GenAI for this course, the discipline, and beyond:

Talk about and evaluate capabilities of GenAI as a group/class
Motivate students to exceed outputs of GenAI
Set expectations early, ideally on day one of class, and provide regular reminders
Policies will vary between campuses, departments, and even individual classes. Each instructor must clearly articulate their own expectations and policies for GenAI use.
When developing your policies, think about what you actually care about, what you actually want to assess, etc.
Maximize trust of students to use the tools effectively and ethically, without relying on them entirely
Ethics guidance on GenAI for students
Be explicit about GenAI policies within syllabus language (“In this course…”)
In courses that allow GenAI on some, but not all assignments, be sure to communicate the expectations in each assignment (“For this assignment…”)
Course Policies & Syllabi Statements
Recommended Course Policies, Evals, Strategies to Promote Academic Honesty
Set and define course policies for disclosure and citation of genAI use
MLA Citing Generative AI
APA How to Cite ChatGPT
Introduction to Academic Integrity (U-M Library page)
Academic Misconduct Policies
Current definitions of academic misconduct may not take account of the new technologies and should be revised as necessary. The same is true of Honor Codes and the policies followed by the Academic Judiciary. The Library’s website offers a basic definition of plagiarism: “Plagiarism: presenting others' work without adequate acknowledgement of its source, as though it were one’s own.” LSA’s website details a range of misconduct, including cheating, plagiarism, falsification of documents, and unacceptable collaboration. The College of Engineering has an Honor Code that defines misconduct. These and other schools’ and colleges’ policies should be updated this summer to take into account the potential and risks of GenAI in instructional contexts.

Common approaches to updating academic misconduct policies are to consider GenAI as prohibited help from another “person” (e.g., UCLA), or as a “source” that should be acknowledged (e.g., UW Madison). The “person” approach misleadingly attributes sentience and a reasoning capacity to GenAI. The “source” approach is more workable.

Treating GenAI as a source that should be acknowledged is more complicated than citing a print book or online article. Unauthorized GenAI use may constitute cheating (a student presenting chatbot outputs as their own original work) and/or plagiarism (copying output from a source without acknowledging that source). U-M schools and colleges will have to determine what misconduct policies will work in their contexts, in consultation with Academic Judiciary bodies.

Some American schools’ academic misconduct policies recommend that instructors use AI-detection tools. This committee finds the detecting tools unreliable and capable of false positives, so we recommend against that approach.

The use of GenAI in coursework is banned at some universities. This approach is impossible to enforce perfectly, partly because detecting tools are (at present) untrustworthy, and partly because GenAI can be used undetectably at any stage in composing processes, such as prompting chatbots to generate ideas, an abstract, an outline, or an essay draft. If GenAI is to be banned in specific contexts, it is vital to ensure that the instruction protects equity and accessibility for students.
